=== 475c84f 2026-09-03
svalboard: measure which symbols earn layer 0, and place them by search

The seven promoted symbols were argued one at a time in build.py's comments,
and three of those arguments had expired against the corpus that now exists.
`@`, `~` and `&` rank 31st, 28th and 27th among symbols at 0.05, 0.18 and 0.19
per 1000 characters, while `` ` ``, `*`, `_` and `=` -- at 5.52, 4.42, 4.24 and
2.11 -- were not on the layer at all. Backtick alone is 102x `@`.

26 alphas and tab hold 27 of the 40 finger keys, so there are exactly 13 symbol
seats. Nothing is demoted to make this work: the seat count is unchanged and
only the occupants move. Every symbol off the layer costs two keystrokes, a
shift pair or MO(1), and every one on it costs one, so the right 13 are the 13
most frequent -- worth 14.74 keystrokes per 1000 characters, ~1.5% of all
typing. `(` and `)` land at ranks 12 and 13, so the pair stays together.

Two expired arguments, both recorded in the README because they failed in
instructive ways. `@` and `~` took ring outer laterals on the reasoning that an
empty key "displaces nothing and still beats two"; sval.yml scores both of those
99, against 2+3 for a hold plus a decent key, so each was a loss of ~17 per 1000
characters. And `~` earned its lateral on ZERO consecutive repeats, true of the
corpus then and 38.3% now -- `~~strikethrough~~` came with the Discord export.

Placement inside the 13 seats is the annealer's. With the alphas pinned, three
of four restarts returned it identically, which is why it is trusted where four
earlier unconstrained runs -- which disagreed with each other from identical
inputs -- were discarded. `f`, `v` and `l` rotate on the left hand, the only
alpha change and worth 264 of the ~400 points any letter movement can buy; the
next ten alpha keys are worth ~11 each.

838.50 -> 235.22 on the same corpus and config, and Character Constraints --
every hand-authored placement rule in the evaluation config -- reaches zero for
the first time.

optimize.py stops carrying a hardcoded inventory to match: promoted_symbols()
ranks it, blended_rates() gives one weighted number per character and drops
empty corpora rather than counting them as zero, and PERMUTING is derived from
the layout instead of listed. FIXED is now empty -- it held six keys for scope
reasons that no longer exist, and a pinned key is one the search cannot examine.

=== f417638 2026-09-01
svalboard: place the promoted symbols by measured frequency, not by feel

The previous commit promoted five symbols on my guess about how often I type
them. Two of those guesses were wrong, so this measures instead.

Two corpora, both filtered to what I actually typed. Hand-typed text: user
messages from 347 Claude Code sessions, after excluding 232 agent-seeded ones
and all tool results, hook injections and pastes, plus zsh history. Code: lines
added by me across five repos. Per 1000 characters:

           -      :     ( )     &      *
  code    11.6   9.3    4.9    0.68   6.7
  typed   33.5   5.1    0.30   0.17   0.03

- `&` was the worst thing on the base layer and I had put it on the index's
  East, one of the strongest cells. It moves to the right ring's East. Ring
  laterals are the hardest cups to reach here, which is what a symbol at
  0.68/1k should be occupying.
- `:` takes the index's East instead. It is the most frequent symbol still
  costing two keys, and the number survives context-checking: 47% of it is
  `key: value` in yaml/json/nix and 16% slices and ternaries, against 27%
  prose colon. Blanked on layer 1, where Arensito had it.
- `*` was rejected. It looks like 6.7/1k in code, but 90% of those occurrences
  are `**` in markdown prose -- much of it agent-written -- and it is 0.03/1k
  in anything hand-typed. Real `*` is below `&`.
- `j` keeps the right pinky's East. It looked like a rare letter squatting on a
  good key, but at 1.04/1k in code and 2.06/1k typed it beats real `*` several
  times over.

`(` and `)` also move off the left ring, which they should never have had: the
ring laterals are the worst keys on this board, and parens at 4.9/1k in code
are not a symbol to put there. They take the middles' outward laterals -- left
middle West, right middle East -- a mirror pair that makes `()` alternate hands
instead of rolling along one finger group.

Promotions remain promotions, not copies: all six vacated Arensito cells are
KC_NO. `;` and `/` are still on both layers; left as-is for now.

=== 9e0b65a 2026-09-01
svalboard: promote `~` to the left ring's West

Takes the lateral `@` deliberately left open, on the argument `@` set: both ring
laterals were empty, so a key here displaces nothing and one beats two even on a
bad key. Measured with freq.py -- 0.12 per 1000 hand-typed characters against
`@`'s 0.06, and 0.22 in code against its 0.33. Same order of magnitude, ahead on
the typed side.

It suits a bad key for a reason the rate does not show. 338 occurrences in the
hand-typed corpus, ZERO of them consecutive repeats, longest run 1: `~` is hit
once at the front of a path and left alone. A key you never hit twice in a row
is the right thing to put somewhere awkward.

`` ` `` was the other candidate and is rejected, for the opposite reason to `*`.
It is the strongest promotion case on the board -- 8.34/1k hand-typed and 3.58
in code, ahead of both `:` and `(`, which hold good keys -- and there is nowhere
to put it. The only free slot was a ring lateral, which is exactly what "nothing
frequent goes on a ring lateral" excludes, and backtick comes in pairs around
inline code spans, so it would be the worst key here hit twice per span. It
stays on MO(1) at the left pinky's West, at least an alternation against the
right-thumb MO(1). Promoting it would mean demoting a letter -- z, q and j are
the only cheaper occupants left -- and a thumb hold mid-word for "jazz" is worse
than the hold it saves. Written down in the README so the next pass does not
re-derive it and reach for the ring lateral anyway.

Its layer-1 lateral is KC_NO, not dropped: dropping the entry falls through to
layer 0's `-` on that key, which is worse than a dead one. That leaves the
layer-1 laterals one shorter and breaks the `~`-beside-`` ` `` pairing, both
noted.

=== 861a64c 2026-09-01
svalboard: promote `@` to the left ring's East

`@` cost MO(1)+key. It is the rarest symbol I measured -- 0.17 per 1000
characters of code written here against `&`'s 1.10, and 0.01 in hand-typed text
against `&`'s 0.19 -- and most of even that 0.17 is `@types/...` imports and
`git@github.com`, which get completed rather than typed. On frequency alone it
stays on the symbol layer.

It moves anyway, because here the promotion is free. Both ring laterals were
empty: `(` and `)` vacated them two commits ago and nothing wanted the slot `g`
left behind, since ring laterals are the hardest cups on this board to reach.
So `@` costs one bad key instead of two good ones and displaces nothing. East
is the inward lateral of the two; West stays free for whatever has to go
somewhere next.

Promoted, not copied -- Arensito's `@` on the left middle's East is KC_NO, so
the duplicate guard still holds. That cell would fall through to `v`, hence the
new letter in the layer-1 dead-key list.

Counted the same way as f417638: Claude Code user turns filtered to typed
human prompts with system-reminders, hook blocks and pastes stripped, plus zsh
history; and lines added by me across drovr, dotfiles, quite-app, kube and
mcloud with vendored trees and lockfiles excluded. The absolute numbers in that
pass differ slightly from f417638's, so the README says to read the `@`/`&` gap
rather than compare columns across passes.

=== 157531b 2026-09-01
svalboard: promote - ( ) & to the base layer, _ onto space

Five symbols were costing MO(1) that shouldn't. Each moves to a free lateral
on layer 0, or to a thumb, and is blanked where Arensito had it -- promoted,
not copied. Nothing is on two keys.

- `-` was already on the base layer's left pinky East and duplicated on
  layer 1. Hands Down Neu publishes `-` on the right inner column; this port
  puts `;` there following the Glove80, which evicted it. The lateral is now
  its only seat, and the rationale is written down where it wasn't before.
- `(` and `)` take the left ring's West and East. That East is the slot `g`
  vacated when it moved to the index's West -- a stale comment from an earlier
  iteration already claimed `(` for it, and now that's true. West is
  screen-left on both hands, so `( )` reads in the order you type it.
- `&` takes the right index East, the strongest of the three free right-hand
  laterals, balancing three promotions that all landed on the left.
- `_` takes the left thumb's space key under MO(1). Arensito puts it on the
  right index's North, the same hand as MO(1) on the right thumb, so
  snake_case was a same-hand contortion; now it's a left-right roll. The cost
  is that space isn't typeable while MO(1) is held. Every other thumb stays
  transparent, so shift, ctrl, enter and backspace still work on the layer.

The five vacated Arensito cells are KC_NO, not KC_TRNS: transparent would fall
through and quietly type n, ., e, i and / from the middle of the symbol layer.

thumb_col() is new -- thumb_row() validates a whole cluster at once and can't
express a single-key override, and the file's standing rule is that thumb
positions are named by physical x, never by column index.

=== 36d2796 2026-09-03
svalboard: one definition of a symbol seat, and a docstring that is still true

Review findings, type-design angle.

  "The 'floating symbol seat' predicate is duplicated between start_layout and
  main instead of being one named function"

Extracted as symbol_seats(). The two copies had to agree exactly -- start_layout
fills the seats, main counts them to size the promoted_symbols request -- and if
they ever drifted the search would be handed a board with a glyph missing and
would report an improvement on it.

The module docstring had also gone stale in the exact way this whole change is
about: it still described 7 floating symbols and six keys pinned by --fix, both
untrue since FIXED emptied. A comment that outlives its premise is what put `@`
and `~` on 99-cost keys in the first place.

Deferred, quoted so nobody meets it as a bug:

  "'_chars' sentinel key mixed into the char->rate dict; each new consumer must
  know and skip the magic string"

Correct, and not fixed here. `_chars` is freq.rates' existing published shape,
read by aggregate_payload and by the README's per-corpus tables; changing it is
a freq.py change with its own callers, not part of this one. blended_rates does
strip it, so nothing downstream of THIS module sees it, and that is pinned by
test_the_chars_bookkeeping_key_is_not_a_character.

1	# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols
2	
3	Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.
4	
5	## Load it
6	
7	1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) with the Svalboard plugged in.
8	2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.
9	
10	No reflash — Vial writes the keymap live.
11	
12	Needs `/dev/hidraw*` to be readable, which it isn't by default. The udev rule is
13	in `system/etc/udev/rules.d/92-vial.rules`. Without it, KeyBard and Vial both see
14	the keyboard and then silently fail to open it.
15	
16	## Layers
17	
18	Each finger sits in a cup with five switches: **N**orth, **S**outh, **E**ast,
19	**W**est and **C**enter (the plain down-press). East is screen-right on both
20	hands, so West is inward on the right hand and outward on the left.
21	
22	### Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu
23	
24	```
25	             W    N     C     S     E
26	  L pinky    tab  w     r     x     "
27	  L ring     )    v     s     c     =
28	  L middle   *    m     n     f     l
29	  L index    g    p     t     d     b
30	  R index    .    `     a     u     '
31	  R middle   -    q     e     o     _
32	  R ring     ,    /     i     y     (
33	  R pinky    z    :     h     k     j
34	```
35	
36	The alphas are Hands Down Neu as it sits on the Glove80, with three exceptions
37	and one structural departure.
38	
39	- **`f`, `v` and `l` rotate.** `f` takes the left middle's South, `v` the ring's
40	  North, `l` the middle's East. `f` is one of the config's high-frequency double
41	  consonants and a ring North is a position its constraint table scores 10 --
42	  `ff` is 11.5% of `f` presses here and 12.0% in English, so this is not an
43	  artifact of one corpus. These three keys are worth 264 points; the next ten
44	  alpha keys are worth about 11 each.
45	- **`g` is on the index's West.** Hands Down gives the left index the whole inner
46	  column (`v`/`b`/`g`). Only two fit on an index cup, so it keeps `b` and `g`.
47	- **`z` and `tab` are on laterals.** They live in outer columns the Svalboard
48	  does not have. `tab` gets the left pinky's West, x=0.0, the outermost point of
49	  the hand -- and it stays there by hand, because tab has no frequency in the
50	  corpus, so the optimizer reads it as free and parks it on the worst key.
51	
52	### The thirteen symbols are measured, not argued
53	
54	26 alphas and tab occupy 27 of the 40 finger keys. The remaining **13 are symbol
55	seats**, and which 13 symbols fill them is decided by `freq.py` against the
56	corpus actually typed here -- agent prompts, shell history, Slack, fourteen
57	years of Discord, and the text tracked in this repo. Per 1000 characters:
58	
59	| in | `-` | `.` | `/` | `'` | `` ` `` | `,` | `*` | `:` | `_` | `"` | `=` | `)` | `(` |
60	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
61	| | 14.07 | 9.20 | 9.19 | 7.78 | 5.52 | 5.40 | 4.42 | 4.29 | 4.24 | 3.27 | 2.11 | 1.68 | 1.63 |
62	
63	| out | `;` | `&` | `~` | `@` |
64	|---|---|---|---|---|
65	| | 1.14 | 0.19 | 0.18 | 0.05 |
66	
67	Every symbol off this layer costs two keystrokes -- a shift pair or `MO(1)` --
68	and every one on it costs one, so the right 13 are simply the 13 most frequent.
69	`` ` `` alone is **102x `@`**. The trade is worth **14.74 keystrokes per 1000
70	characters**, about 1.5% of everything typed.
71	
72	`(` and `)` both make the cut, at ranks 12 and 13, so the pair stays together.
73	
74	**Two earlier arguments on this layer have expired**, and both are worth
75	recording because they were wrong in instructive ways:
76	
77	- `@` and `~` were promoted onto the ring outer laterals on the reasoning that
78	  those keys were empty, so a symbol there "displaces nothing and still beats
79	  two". It does not. `config/keyboard/sval.yml` scores both of those laterals
80	  **99**, against 2+3 for a hold plus a decent key -- so each promotion was a
81	  loss of roughly 17 per 1000 characters, not a free win. A key nobody wants is
82	  not the same as a key that is free.
83	- `~` earned its lateral on a count of **zero** consecutive repeats. That was
84	  true of the corpus available at the time. It is **38.3%** now: the Discord
85	  export arrived carrying `~~strikethrough~~`. The measurement was honest and
86	  the conclusion still expired, which is the argument for deriving this from a
87	  corpus that gets rebuilt rather than from a comment.
88	
89	Placement within the 13 seats is the annealer's, not hand-argued. With the
90	alphas pinned, three of four restarts returned this arrangement identically --
91	which is what makes it worth trusting, where four earlier unconstrained runs
92	disagreed with each other from identical inputs and were discarded.
93	
94	`?` and `~` stay reachable as shift+`/` and shift+`` ` ``, both now on this
95	layer. `;` is on `MO(1)`; `@` and `&` moved to the left pinky's laterals there,
96	because `check_symbols()` fails the build on any symbol costing three keys.
97	
98	Against the layout this replaces, scored on the same corpus and config:
99	**838.50 to 235.22**, and Character Constraints -- every hand-authored placement
100	rule in the evaluation config -- reaches **zero** for the first time.
101	
102	### Layer 1 — Arensito symbols (hold `MO(1)`)
103	
104	```
105	  { } [ ] ·   · · < > $
106	  ; / · 0 ·   \ 1 · · =
107	  6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
108	```
109	
110	Ported from the Glove80 `symbols` layer. `·` is a dead key — Arensito puts
111	`-`, `:`, `&`, `@`, `_`, `(` and `)` there, and all seven are one-key elsewhere
112	now (see layer 0 and the thumbs below). They're dead rather than transparent on
113	purpose: falling through would type `n`, `.`, `e`, `i`, `b`, `v` and `/` from
114	the middle of the symbol layer.
115	
116	The grid above is on N/C/S; the
117	laterals carry the six symbols Arensito leaves out, which would otherwise cost
118	`MO(1)`+shift+key:
119	
120	```
121	  ` on the left pinky        ! on the left index
122	  % on the left ring         # on the left middle
123	  | on the right index       ^ on the right middle
124	```
125	
126	`@` and `&` are here, on the left pinky's two laterals. Both came *off* layer 0
127	in the symbol reshuffle, and both are shift+digit with the digits on this layer
128	— so without a seat here each would cost `MO(1)`+shift+key. `check_symbols()`
129	fails the build on exactly that, which is how this was caught rather than
130	shipped.
131	
132	`` ` `` used to hold the left pinky's West and is on layer 0 now; a promoted
133	symbol is never copied, so the seat went to `@`. `~` is no longer on either
134	layer as a key: it is shift+`` ` ``, which costs two keys now that grave has a
135	base-layer seat.
136	
137	`?` isn't here on purpose — it's shift+`/`, and `/` is on the base layer.
138	
139	`_` gets a second seat on the **left thumb's space key**. Arensito's own `_` is
140	on the right index's North, the same hand as `MO(1)`; on space it's a
141	left-right roll instead. Space itself isn't typeable while `MO(1)` is held —
142	every other thumb stays transparent, so shift, ctrl, enter and backspace still
143	work on the layer.
144	
145	### Layer 2 — navigation (hold `MO(2)`)
146	
147	Arrows four-across on the right hand, innermost to outermost, matching Glove80
148	base-layer positions 75–78:
149	
150	```
151	  R index  R middle  R ring  R pinky
152	     ←        ↓        ↑        →
153	```
154	
155	F1–F12, home/end, pgup/pgdn, volume and play/pause fill the rest.
156	
157	`MO(2)` is on the right thumb's **nail** so that `alt` can be held with it — see
158	"Thumbs" below. Everything else on the layer is a right-hand finger, so shift,
159	ctrl and GUI reach it from the left thumb without contortion.
160	
161	### Layer 15 — mouse
162	
163	Svalboard's firmware switches here by itself when the pointing device moves, and
164	leaves on the first key that isn't on this layer. **Nothing reaches it by
165	keypress, by design.** Buttons 1/3/2 sit on index/middle/ring South of both
166	hands; `USER06` is `SV_RECALIBRATE_POINTER`.
167	
168	"Leaves on the first key that isn't on this layer" is true, and is not the same
169	as a way out. Eight cups are taken — index, middle and ring South on both hands
170	plus both pinky Centers — so if the first thing you type after nudging the
171	pointer is `d`, `f`, `c`, `r`, `u`, `o`, `y` or `h`, it clicks or recalibrates
172	instead. The layer leaves, having eaten the keystroke.
173	
174	**The right thumb's double-down is `TO(0)`** — the exit that costs no character.
175	Three things about that choice:
176	
177	- **Not a Svalboard keycode**, because there isn't one. All twenty `USER*`
178	  codes in the keyboard's `vial.json` are pointer settings, scroll modes and
179	  layer toggles; the nearest, `SV_TOGGLE_AUTOMOUSE`, switches auto-activation
180	  off altogether rather than dismissing one visit.
181	- **`TO(0)`, not `TO(15)`.** QMK's auto-mouse intercepts a `TO()` aimed at the
182	  mouse layer itself and reads it as *pin this layer on* — the opposite. A
183	  `TO()` at any other layer isn't intercepted, so it falls through to a plain
184	  `layer_move(0)` that clears 15 outright. Nothing desyncs:
185	  `auto_mouse_layer_off()` tests real layer state rather than a cached flag, so
186	  the next movement of the pointer brings the layer straight back.
187	- **Right double-down**, which is `ralt` on layer 0 and the least missed key on
188	  the cluster while a hand is on the pointer. The left double-down keeps
189	  `delete` deliberately: select with the pointer, press delete, and the delete
190	  both lands *and* leaves the layer. An exit key there would swallow it and
191	  cost a second press.
192	
193	### Thumbs
194	
195	The cluster is not six keys laid out in space. It is six switches hit by
196	different **parts of the same thumb**, and the `.vil` column index — which *is*
197	mirrored between hands, unlike the x coordinate — names them:
198	
199	| col | part | left | right |
200	|---|---|---|---|
201	| 0 | knuckle | ctrl | **alt** (one-shot) |
202	| 1 | nail | gui | **`MO(2)`** |
203	| 2 | down | shift | `MO(1)` |
204	| 3 | pad | space | bspc |
205	| 4 | up | esc | enter |
206	| 5 | double-down | delete | ralt (`TO(0)` on layer 15) |
207	
208	`pad` is the community favourite and holds the most-pressed thumb key on each
209	hand. `down` takes the heaviest hold. `knuckle` is the worst key on the cluster
210	and is exactly where a modifier belongs. `up` strains under heavy use, so it
211	gets taps rather than holds.
212	
213	**One thumb holds one of these at a time.** The exception is a *fat-finger*
214	pair, of which knuckle+nail is the reliable one — the only way a single thumb
215	holds two thumb keys at once.
216	
217	That is the whole reason `MO(2)` sits on the nail. It used to be on `up`, and
218	that made `alt`+arrow — `alt+shift+down`, `ctrl+alt+left`, all of them — not
219	awkward but **unpressable**: alt is on the knuckle, and no thumb reaches knuckle
220	and up together. Moving `MO(2)` to the nail puts it on alt's fat-finger partner
221	and costs only `enter`, which took `up` in exchange. Enter is a tap and pays
222	`up`'s strain once; `MO(2)` is a hold and was paying it for the length of every
223	arrow key.
224	
225	**Alt is a one-shot**, `OSM(MOD_LALT)`, because one chord partner is not enough.
226	The knuckle pairs with the nail and nothing else, so alt can chord with exactly
227	one right-thumb key — and `MO(2)`, `enter` and `bspc` all want to be it. Sticky
228	alt sidesteps the whole problem: tap it and it holds for the next key, so
229	`M-RET` and `M-DEL` work without a chord at all. `M-DEL` has never been
230	available on this layout by any other route — backspace is on the pad. Holding
231	it is unchanged, so `alt+tab` still cycles.
232	
233	That is one of the three fixes the Svalboard community names for this squeeze.
234	The other two don't fit here: **one layer hold per thumb** (this layout has both
235	on the right) and **bottom-row mods**, "because south is so good on sval" —
236	South is alphas here. The underlying rule being broken is *modifiers on one
237	thumb, layer switches on the other*: `alt`, `MO(1)` and `MO(2)` are all on the
238	right. Shift, ctrl and GUI escape it by being left-thumb keys. Alt can't follow
239	them; the left thumb's six seats are full.
240	
241	Note `OSM(MOD_LALT)`, not `OSM(KC_LALT)` — Vial accepts both, but they are
242	different keycodes (`0x52A8` vs `0x52E3`) and the latter reloads as raw hex.
243	
244	`double-down` is not a sixth position. It is the `down` key pressed harder, the
245	DataHand deep press. That is why nothing you press in a hurry goes there — `gui`
246	sat on both and was unusable, `tab` was tried and was worse. They now hold
247	`delete` and `ralt`. Those two slots were found empirically, as "the only
248	positions with no free side", well before the mechanism had a name.
249	
250	Layer 15's `TO(0)` on the right double-down does not break that rule. The rule
251	is about keys hit reflexively, mid-word, in flow. Leaving mouse mode is the
252	opposite: a deliberate hand-off between two things you were doing, with the
253	pause already in it.
254	
255	`space` left and `bspc` right match Glove80 positions 69 and 74 — Svalboard's own
256	configs ship those mirrored.
257	
258	## Printable cheatsheet
259	
260	```sh
261	python3 cheatsheet.py   # writes cheatsheet.html
262	```
263	
264	Open it and print: one portrait Letter page, layers 0, 1 and 2 drawn at the
265	hardware's own key positions, with the layer-15 note in the footer. On layers 1
266	and 2, keys that fall through to layer 0 are printed faint rather than left
267	blank — under `MO(1)` shift, ctrl, enter and backspace are all still live, and
268	an empty box would say otherwise.
269	
270	There is no second copy of the layout in it: `cheatsheet.py` imports `build.py`
271	and reads the emitted layers, so the sheet cannot disagree with the `.vil`. Two
272	guards, on top of `build.py`'s four:
273	
274	- **Labels.** Every live keycode must have a glyph. Adding a key to `build.py`
275	  without labelling it aborts the build instead of printing a blank box.
276	- **Page width.** The board must fit inside the printable width at the declared
277	  margins. Too wide looks fine on screen — the browser viewport is whatever size
278	  it is — and only shows up as a shrunken printout after you've walked to the
279	  printer.
280	
281	## Measuring what actually gets typed
282	
283	```sh
284	python3 freq.py            # refresh the corpus, report the promoted set
285	python3 freq.py '`' '~'    # rates for specific characters, with context checks
286	python3 freq.py --all      # every printable ASCII symbol
287	```
288	
289	The promotions above are argued from measured frequency, and this is what
290	measures it: prompts you typed (sidechains and machine-injected blocks dropped),
291	zsh history, and the tracked text files in this repo, reported per 1000
292	characters.
293	
294	**The corpus is cached in `~/.local/share/svalboard-freq/` and must never be
295	committed** — it is shell history and work prompts, and this repo is public.
296	What is safe to publish is the aggregate, so `freq.py` writes `freq.json` here:
297	per-character rates only, which say nothing about content.
298	
299	Two context checks come with it, because a raw rate lies in exactly the way
300	`*` lied. Prompts are split inside/outside ``` fences, since a rate driven by
301	fenced blocks is driven by pasting rather than typing; the code corpus is split
302	by file extension, since a symbol confined to one file type is a symbol you type
303	in one context.
304	
305	One caveat on comparing against the table above: those numbers are weighted
306	toward shell history, and `freq.py`'s combined figure is dominated by the prompt
307	corpus, which is ~18x larger. The ordering agrees, the absolute values do not.
308	Compare like with like — the per-corpus columns, not the blend.
309	
310	## Regenerating
311	
312	```sh
313	python3 build.py
314	```
315	
316	`build.py` emits the entire `.vil`. There is no base file to patch and no
317	network access — every layer, keycode and piece of Vial metadata is declared in
318	it. It was cut over from a patch-the-Colemak-config approach by diffing against
319	the old output until byte-identical, so the rewrite carried nothing over by
320	accident.
321	
322	Four guards, any of which aborts the build:
323	
324	- **Geometry.** `CUP_XY` holds the physical position of all 40 finger switches,
325	  read out of the keyboard's own `vial.json` over the Vial protocol. The build
326	  asserts North is above Center, South below, East right and West left, for
327	  every cup. Get the column order wrong and you still emit a structurally
328	  perfect file with every key in the wrong place — this is the check that
329	  catches it, and it checks against the hardware rather than another config's
330	  conventions.
331	- **Coverage.** All 26 letters and 10 digits reachable, plus space, backspace,
332	  enter, tab and grave. Grave has no shift-fallback and went missing once when
333	  Arensito's `{` landed on top of it.
334	- **Symbol cost.** No printable ASCII symbol may require `MO(1)`+shift+key.
335	- **Duplicates.** Nothing on the base layer reachable from two positions.
336	  Moving a key by adding an override leaves the original behind unless it's
337	  blanked; that put `g` on two cups once.
338	
339	Thumb rows are declared by physical x, not column index, and the build fails if
340	the declared positions don't match the hardware. The indices are **not** mirrored
341	between hands — left column 3 is at x=7.9 and mirrors right column *4* at
342	x=13.6, not right column 3 at x=14.1. Reasoning about them directly produced one
343	wrong answer already.
344	
345	## Source
346	
347	Glove80 layout `e3409150-bb22-49c0-8614-10035f3f6a04` ("Sauyon layout
348	2026-01-20"), layers `Base` and `symbols`. Its grids are transcribed into

350	
351	Custom `USER*` keycode names (`SV_SCROLL_TOGGLE`, `SV_TOGGLE_AUTOMOUSE`, the
352	sniper modes, DPI controls) come from the keyboard itself — Vial command
353	`0xFE 0x02` returns an LZMA-compressed `vial.json` describing them.

## What actually happened

`475c84f` threw out every hand-argued symbol placement at once. Two changes did it:

1. **Which symbols get layer 0 became a measurement.** 26 alphas + tab = 27 of 40 finger keys → exactly 13 symbol seats, filled by the top 13 by corpus frequency.
2. **`FIXED` was emptied** (`optimize.py:100`) — previously `, . / ; " '` were pinned. With nothing pinned, the annealer placed all 13.

## Why `~` and `;` left layer 0

Pure rank. Neither was moved to a bad key — both fell off:

- **`;` — 1.14/1k, rank 14.** Missed the cut by exactly one seat. It sat on right ring West; that seat is now `,`. It's on `MO(1)` now.
- **`~` — 0.18/1k, rank 16.** It had held left ring West on the argument that the cell was empty so "a symbol there displaces nothing." Two things killed it: `sval.yml` scores that cell **99** (vs 2+3 for `MO(1)`+key), so it was a ~17/1k *loss*, not a free win; and its other argument — zero consecutive repeats — expired when the Discord export arrived carrying `~~strikethrough~~` (38.3% repeats now). It's shift+`` ` `` today.

## Why `,` and the parens landed where they did

Your own constraint, from `7d0938b6`: *"I don't want to demote characters, just because it doesn't feel nice aesthetically."* That means all 40 finger keys must carry a glyph — and `sval.yml` scores **four cells at 99**: L-pinky N, L-ring W, R-ring E, R-pinky N. Something has to sit on them.

- **`(` and `)` are ranks 12 and 13** — the two cheapest passengers on the layer, so the search sank them into two of the 99s (L-ring W, R-ring E). They came off cost-3 middle laterals. That's the whole mechanism: cheapest symbol gets the unreachable seat.
- **`,` moved R-index W → R-ring W.** The cost model rates *both cells 5*, so the swap looked free to the annealer. Your ring finger disagrees; the model has no term for that.
- You approved the third 99 explicitly — *"r pinky north is totally fine"* — which is `:` at 4.29/1k.

## The wart worth knowing

By the README's own arithmetic — the one used to evict `~` — putting `(` and `)` on 99-cost cells costs **~150 per 1000 chars each** versus leaving them on `MO(1)` at 5. The seat argument counts *keystrokes* (1 vs 2); the eviction argument counts *key costs* (99 vs 5). Those two metrics disagree precisely on the four worst keys, and the parens are sitting in the gap.

Your instinct matches the config on the outward laterals and contradicts it on the inward ones. And neither can currently do anything, because of a structural gap:

## The annealer never compares a cell to a chord

`optimize.py:419` — `seats = len(seats_at)`. The seat count is **geometry**: every free layer-0 cell is a seat, and `promoted_symbols(rank, seats)` is asked for exactly that many symbols. So a cell can only lose to a *different glyph*, never to `MO(1)`. Re-costing ring laterals just reshuffles which of the 13 sits there — `,` would swap with `=`, and that's it.

## What a chord actually costs

`key_costs` is a unigram metric, weight 5.0, linear × frequency. MO(1) is the right thumb's Down = **cost 2** (thumb costs `4, 8, 1, 3, 2, 5` against `Nail, DoubleDown, Pad, Knuckle, Down, Up`). Plus a decent layer-1 key at 3:

| cell | cost | vs chord (5) | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| ring **Out** (L ring W, R ring E) | **99** | 20x worse | `)` `(` |
| ring **In** (L ring E, R ring W) | **5** | break-even | `=` `,` |
| ring North | 6 | slightly worse | `/` |

So the config already agrees the ring Outs are indefensible — it just has no way to act on it. On the ring Ins it gives you nothing: a 5 is exactly a chord, which is why the annealer moved `,` onto one for free. Your claim is that 5 is too low, and that's a recalibration only your hands can supply.

Fixing it means one real change: **gate `symbol_seats()` on cost**, so cells above the chord price stop being seats and go `KC_NO`, with the seat count falling out of the costs instead of the geometry.

**No — three of them are rarer than `=`, and four are rarer than `,`.** Measured on your corpus with the same blend `optimize.py` ranks with:

| glyph | /1k | | glyph | /1k |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `,` | **5.402** | | `"` | 3.268 |
| `*` | 4.420 | | `x` | **2.766** |
| `:` | 4.298 | | `=` | **2.112** |
| `_` | 4.244 | | `)` `(` | 1.674 / 1.632 |
| | | | `j` | **1.545** |
| | | | `z` `q` | **0.552 / 0.529** |

`x` is the only one that clears `=`, and only just. `j` is rarer than both parens. `z` and `q` are below `;` (1.137) — the only things under them on the whole board are `&`, `~` and `@`, all of which you already chord.

## What that means for the choice you just made

The four rarest glyphs on the 40 finger keys are `q`, `z`, `j`, `(`. Under "all four ring laterals go dead," the cells get vacated and `"` `=` `)` `(` — 8.686/1k — go to chords, while `q` `z` `j` keep single-key seats at 2.626/1k combined. Three of the four demoted symbols are more common than three of the alphas that stay.

Straight keystroke price of the no-demotion rule, here: **~7.05 extra keystrokes per 1000 characters**, about 0.7% of typing (8.686 demoted vs 1.632 if `q`/`z`/`j` took three ring laterals and only `(` chorded).

One argument on your side that the rates don't show: `z`, `q` and `j` land **mid-word** — "jazz", "quiz", "fixing". A bad key hurts more there than a chord does on `=` or `"`, which you type deliberately with a pause already in the stroke. That's a real reason for the rule, not only an aesthetic one.

One refinement to what I said earlier: `FIXED = set()` in the committed `optimize.py` is real, but the pin came from an ad-hoc CLI call to the rust binary, not from that constant.

## It was tried, unconstrained, and it does exactly what you'd expect

A ceiling run with nothing pinned returned `zjcbdwxuvy*)sfm"hnrlk\`pgt=_eo/-,iq:□'a(.` — which puts **`z`, `x`, `q` and tab on the four 99 cells** and gives `(`, `)` and `,` decent keys. Your instinct matches the optimizer's.

| unconstrained ceiling | **55.71** | **24 of 26** |

It was rejected for the relearn, not the score, and you'd said *"I'm not huge on completely rewriting my whole layout."*

## The option nobody searched

The rejection used a **pairwise-swap ladder** from the old board, and its knee was at 3 alpha moves (first three swaps worth 88 points each, everything after ~11). Step 7 of that ladder was `g ↔ z` at −19.76 — the closest anyone got to your idea, and it moves `z` to a *good* key, not a ring lateral.

Nobody ran "**unpin only `z`, `q`, `j`, `x`; leave the other 22 alone.**" That's four keys of relearn instead of 24, and it's the exact shape of what you're proposing.

`python3 optimize.py` today passes `--fix` only when `FIXED` is non-empty — and it's empty. So a re-run **would go unconstrained** and return something near the 24-key ceiling. The repo cannot currently reproduce its own shipped layout; the pin exists only in that shell command.

Both of your observations point at the same thing, and it's important enough to stop and say plainly.

**The metric weights:**

| weight | metric | |
|---:|---|---|
| 1000 | `fsb` (full scissors), `manual_bigram_penalty`, `character_constraints` | |
| 500 | `sympathetic` | |
| 150 | `sfb` (same-finger bigrams) | |
| 100 | `hsb`, `weak_redirect` | |
| 50 / 25 / 25 | `finger_balance`, `hand_disbalance`, `sfs` | |
| **5** | **`key_costs`** | ← everything we've been arguing about |
| off | `modifier_usage` | |

**Yes, the Hands Down concerns are accounted for — they *are* the objective.** SFB + FSB alone were 186 of the 226 total. Key cost was 12.56. So the answer to your `l`/`v` surprise is that **the rotation was never about key comfort**: `f` sat on L ring North, which the constraint table scores 10 for a high-frequency double consonant (`ff` is 11.5% of your `f` presses), and getting it off there drove Character Constraints to 0.00 for the first time — worth −161.76 then −102.74. `l` on a cost-3 lateral and `v` on a cost-6 North were the *price* of that, paid at weight 5 against gains at weight 1000.

**Which means the lever I've been pulling is the wrong one.** Recosting ring laterals is a weight-5 nudge. That's why inner 5→8 moved the total by 2 points, and why restart 3 cheerfully put `,` straight back on the ring inner. If "ring laterals are hard to hit" is a real constraint for your hands, it belongs in `character_constraints` at weight 1000 — the config's own mechanism for hand-authored placement rules — not in `key_costs`.

Two caveats on "Hands Down philosophy" specifically: the weights are **jeffzi's** encoding of it in the sval port, not Hands Down's published rationale; and in every run so far the alphas were pinned, so Neu's arrangement was preserved *by construction*, not because the metric endorsed it.

**Step 3 of 5 running** — variant C: parens chorded, ring outers dead, `q` `z` `j` `x` floating.

Two things worth knowing before the number lands:

1. **The optimizer cannot price a chord.** `modifier_usage` is `enabled: false`, so a symbol moved to `MO(1)` doesn't cost the model anything — it just leaves the objective. Variant C's total won't be comparable to 226.27 or 199.64. The chord decision has to be argued in keystrokes: `(` + `)` = **3.31 per 1000 characters**, ~0.33% of typing. That's the whole price, and you've said you'd rather pay it than hit a ring outer.

The breakdown exposes the actual root cause of this entire two-session saga:

**Key Costs: 10.88 → 10.85.** Moving comma from a cost-8 key to a cost-3 key is worth **0.03 points out of 199**. The weight-5 `key_costs` term is numerically incapable of expressing "this key is hard to hit" — a character at 5.4/1000 shifted across five cost units moves the objective by three hundredths. Everything else (the +1.66) is bigram noise pushing back.

So `,` and the parens didn't land on bad keys because anyone argued for it. They landed there because **nothing in the model can object.** The only mechanism with real authority is `character_constraints` at weight 1000 — and it contains no rule about ring laterals.

content.text:
What would you like to clarify?

For context, here's where each question is coming from:

**On the pinky laterals** — I don't have a reading from you on the pinky cup at all. You've told me ring outers are horrible, ring inners feel wrong for something as frequent as `,`, and pinky *North* is fine. Pinky laterals never came up, and the stock config scores R pinky West at 5 — the same number it gave R ring West before I raised it. So I can't tell whether comma at 5.40/1k landing there is a fix or just the same problem one finger over.

**On ring North** — this one may be badly framed. I offered "ban it" and "recost it down" as opposites, but I don't actually know which direction you'd go, and the third option contradicts the second. If ring North is fine, the honest move is to lower it to 4 like the pinky Norths, not to ban anything.

Also worth saying plainly before you answer: the whole board is now resting on numbers I invented. Ring inner 5→8 and both pinky Norths 99→4 were my picks from your descriptions, and the ring-lateral bans are a rule I wrote into a third party's constraint table. None of it is measured against your hands — it's your words, translated by me into a config, and the optimizer will faithfully obey whatever I put there.
wait. should they be banned or just the weight adjusted? I don't like these special rules

Your instinct is right, and the arithmetic says the weight alone can't do it either. Here's the honest accounting:

- `key_costs` weight 5 produces a metric total of 10.88, so Σ(freq × cost) ≈ 2.18 across the whole board.
- Moving comma from cost 8 to cost 3 changes that sum by **0.006** — hence the 0.03-point swing.
- To make that beat the +1.66 the bigram metrics charge for the same move, the weight would need to be **≈280**.
- At weight 280, `key_costs` becomes ~609 points against a 199-point objective. Key cost *becomes* the objective and SFB/FSB stop mattering — you'd delete the Hands Down philosophy to fix comma.

So: not the weight, and I agree not the per-character bans. I added 10 characters × 4 positions to a table that already carries hand-authored exceptions for 14 characters — doubling down on the mechanism you're objecting to, and it's exactly the kind of rule the README says went stale and put `@` and `~` on 99-cost keys in the first place.

**The third option is the cost table itself.** The stock config already scores ring *outers* 99. You've said the inners are wrong for anything frequent. Setting all four ring laterals to 99 is one statement about four cells, names no character, and needs no exceptions — comma then leaves on its own because 5.40/1k × 96 cost units is worth 2.59 points, which clears the 1.66 the bigrams charge.

Your instinct is right, and the cause is one number. **Discord is 26% of the blend, and it's a register where you barely punctuate:**

| corpus | weight | `.` | `,` | `-` | `/` | `'` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| prompts | 0.38 | 13.12 | 7.74 | 10.69 | 4.65 | 1.71 |
| shell | 0.18 | 9.81 | 4.84 | 43.99 | 33.97 | 22.88 |
| code | 0.08 | 12.99 | 6.77 | 15.12 | 6.33 | 3.69 |
| slack | 0.10 | 4.88 | 7.18 | 6.52 | 6.13 | 5.07 |
| **discord** | **0.26** | **3.57** | **1.28** | **0.86** | **0.75** | **8.53** |

Comma is **6× lower** in Discord than in your prompts, period **3.7× lower**. A quarter of the weight comes from text where you write like it's chat — and it drags both punctuation marks down while pushing `'` (contractions) up.

For reference, ordinary English prose runs ~6–10 commas and ~8–11 periods per 1000 characters. Your blend says 5.40 and 9.21 — comma sits *below* the normal English range, which is the anomaly you felt.

**The corpus is depressed but not distorted.** Dropping Discord entirely raises comma 5.40 → 6.85 (+27%) and period 9.21 → 11.19 (+21%), which puts both back inside the normal English range. But the *ranking* — the only thing seat selection uses — barely moves:

`,` is **#6 under every weighting**: as configured, Discord halved, Discord dropped. Period stays #2–3. The only reordering anywhere near the cut is `#` climbing past the parens at #12.

So the corpus isn't what put comma on a bad key. The weight-5 `key_costs` term was. What the corpus *does* change is the strength of the argument for moving it: at 6.85/1k the fix is worth 27% more.

Worth knowing: that 0.26 Discord weight is a hand-set number in `optimize.py`'s `WEIGHTS`, same class as the cell costs and constraint rules you objected to. It's a claim about how much of your day is Discord, not a measurement.

**And the cost-table fix works — no special rules needed.** With all four ring laterals at 99 and the stock constraint table restored (bans thrown away):

```
             W    N     C     S     E
  L pinky   tab  w     r     "     j
  L ring     ·    v     s     c     z     ← z (0.55/1k)
  L middle   *    m     n     f     l
  L index    g    p     t     d     b

  R middle   -    =     e     o     _
  R ring     q    .     i     y     ·     ← q (0.53/1k)

Same outcome as the 40 hand-authored bans, reached by four numbers in the cost table instead. It's actually *better* — it picks `z` (0.55) for the left inner where the ban version picked `x` (2.77).

content.text:
Two things fall out of this, and one of them changes the plan.

**The seat cut moves:** `=` drops 2.12 → 1.56 (#11 → #14) and lands *below* both parens. So under your weights, if the parens chord, `=` should chord too — it's now the rarer one.

**But the bigger one:** if the four rarest alphas take the four ring laterals, then every remaining cell is cost ≤ 6. All 13 symbol seats become decent keys — and the reason to chord the parens disappears, because it was "rather chord than take a horrible key." Nothing horrible is left for them to take.

That would mean: no dead cells, no chording, 13 symbols on ordinary keys, and `q` `z` `j` `x` absorbing the ring laterals. It costs about 2.6 points in the model to park those four letters on 99s, which is cheap.

`freq.py` deliberately has no network and no token; it just reads JSON dumps from `~/.local/share/svalboard-freq/slack/`, accepting either a bare list of message objects or the `{"messages": [...]}` envelope the search API returns. So pulling more means dropping more dumps in that directory.

This session has the Slack MCP, so I can do it directly: `from:@me` sliced into date windows to get past the per-query result cap, one JSON per window, straight into the cache. Twenty-odd monthly windows would plausibly take you from 15k to a few hundred thousand characters — enough that Slack's 0.20 weight stops resting on a 0.1% sample.

You're right on both counts, and my hand-transcription introduced a real error: I replaced URLs with placeholders, and since `freq.py` keeps the *label* half of `<url|label>`, that under-counts `/` and `.` — the two characters this whole question is about. Deleting that file rather than letting it skew the corpus.

**Better fetch route, if you want this reproducible:** a user token (`xoxp-`) with the `search:read` scope calls `search.messages` at **100 results per page** instead of 20, with no model in the loop — roughly 10 calls per 1000 messages against my ~50. Create an app at api.slack.com/apps, add `search:read` as a *user* scope, install, and put the token in sops like your other secrets. Then a small `slack_pull.py` does the whole corpus in one command, and `freq.py` stays network-free and tokenless by design. That's the version worth having; the MCP grind is a one-off.

For now, handing the grind to a subagent so it doesn't land in my context:

input.prompt:
Build up a local Slack corpus for a keyboard-layout frequency analysis. This is Sauyon's own Slack messages, pulled into a local cache directory. The cache is never committed and only aggregate per-character rates ever leave it.

## Tool

Load the Slack search tool first:
  ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude_ai_Slack__slack_search_public_and_private"

Sauyon's Slack user_id is U0A9ZHCGHDJ.

Call it like this:
  query: "from:<@U0A9ZHCGHDJ> during:2026-08"
  limit: 20            (20 is the hard max)
  sort: "timestamp"
  include_context: false
  response_format: "concise"

The response includes a `pagination_info` with a cursor. Pass that back as `cursor` to get the next page of the SAME query. Keep paging a month until the cursor stops coming back or you have taken 15 pages of that month, then move to the next month.

## Coverage

Work backwards month by month: 2026-01, then 2025-12, 2025-11, ... back to 2024-01. Also go back and take deeper pages (pages 2 onward) for 2026-02 through 2026-08, which currently only have page 1 pulled.

Budget roughly 200-250 tool calls total. Stop early if months come back empty (that is the start of the employment history).

## Parsing

Results come back as numbered lines like:

  1. #channel-name - Sauyon Lee: the message text here 2026-08-31 21:57:43 PDT
  2. DM with Someone, Sauyon Lee - Sauyon Lee: another message 2026-08-31 17:59:19 PDT

A message may span multiple lines; a new message always starts with a line matching ^\d+\.  — use that as the record separator.

For each record: strip the leading "N. " numbering, strip the "<channel or DM description> - Sauyon Lee: " prefix (everything up to and including the first "Sauyon Lee: "), and strip the trailing " YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS PDT|PST" timestamp.

TRANSCRIBE THE MESSAGE TEXT VERBATIM. Do not redact, shorten, or substitute URLs, channel names, or anything else. The whole point is an accurate character-frequency count, and rewriting a URL changes the rates for "/" and "." which is exactly what is being measured. Slack's own markup (<@U123|name>, <#C123|chan>, <url|label>) must be preserved exactly as it appears — the consuming script has its own regexes to handle those.

## Output

Write one JSON file per month into ~/.local/share/svalboard-freq/slack/ named like:
  from-me-2025-11.json

Each file must be this exact shape:
  {"messages": [{"text": "..."}, {"text": "..."}]}

Write with json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False). Create the directory if needed. Do NOT write anything into any git repository, and do not run git commands.

## Report back

Report ONLY aggregate numbers — for each month: the filename, the message count, and the total character count, plus a grand total. Do NOT include any message content, channel names, or people's names in your final report. Keep it under 30 lines.

Running. Two things about this that I'd rather say now than have look arbitrary later.

**`#` and `?` are 14th and 15th by frequency** — they only reach the board because you pulled the parens off it. The pipeline still selects the 13 *most* frequent and the annealer still sinks the *rarest of those 13* onto the worst cells, so nothing is hand-picked. But it does mean the two ring outers will be holding glyphs that lost the seat competition on their own merits.

**Both already cost exactly two keystrokes**, so this is a real trade, not free: `?` is shift+`/` with `/` on layer 0, and `#` is `MO(1)`+lateral. Giving either a 99 cell swaps two easy presses for one awful one. By the cost model it's a loss for any glyph — 99 against ~5 — which is why the model wanted those cells empty. Filling them is your call over the model's, and picking the rarest glyphs is what makes the loss smallest.

If "rarest" is what you actually want there, `;` (1.205) and `|` (1.274) are rarer still than `#` and `?`. They don't get picked because `promoted_symbols()` takes the top N by frequency — selecting them instead would need a hand rule, which is the thing you've twice told me not to add. Say the word if you'd rather have the hand rule; otherwise this stays derived.

One redundancy to note: with a dedicated `?` key *and* `/` on layer 0, `?` becomes reachable two ways. `build.py`'s duplicate guard won't fire — different keycodes — but the README currently argues `?` is deliberately absent precisely because shift+`/` already covers it. **`@` and `~` are the rarest things you type**, at 0.071 and 0.200 per 1000. `#` at 1.409 is twenty times more common than `@`. And `@` and `~` are precisely what the previous session had sitting on those ring outer laterals — and what `475c84f` demoted, calling it an expired argument.

# TDD

## Overview

**Test-first, always.** Write the failing test before the code it covers, watch
it fail, then write the minimal code to make it pass. A test you never saw fail
proves nothing — it may pass for the wrong reason, or not exercise the behavior
at all.

Keep the test scoped to the interfaces you are actually changing — a test that
drifts wider stops being a contract anyone can rely on. Inside a drovr phase
this also binds the next phase's contract.

## The cycle

1. **RED** — write the failing test named in the task's verification. Run it.
   *Watch it fail*, and confirm it fails for the reason you expect (missing
   behavior, not a typo or compile error elsewhere).
2. **GREEN** — write the *minimal* code to make that test pass. No extra
   features, no speculative abstraction — just enough to go green.
3. **REFACTOR** — clean up with the test as your safety net, re-running it.

Repeat per behavior. One failing test at a time.

## Red flags — STOP

- Wrote code before the test → delete it, start with the test.
- "I'll add the test after" → tests-after check *what the code does*, not what it
  *should* do. Test first.
- Test passed the first time you ran it → you never saw RED; make sure it truly
  exercises the new behavior.
- Test is scoped wider than this task's interfaces → tighten it; drift breaks the
  contract the next phase inherits.

## Verifying the pass

Green on the one test is necessary, not sufficient. Before claiming done, hand
off to `drovr:verification-before-completion` — run the full suite and the build,
and confirm with evidence, not assertion.

    """Slack's wire format back to the characters a person actually pressed.

    Two things happen here and the second one is the point. Entities and bare
    URLs come out: a mention is a click in a picker and a pasted URL is a

    README spends a paragraph placing. Unescape `&` last so a literal

def mention_sigil(match):
    """The one character a person pressed to open a mention picker.

    Shared by both chat loaders because both had the same bug: the entity was
    deleted whole, so a ping counted as zero keystrokes. It is one -- `@` for a
    user, role or broadcast, `#` for a channel -- and at Sauyon's rates that
    single character is the difference between `@` reading as the rarest symbol
    on the board and reading as mid-tail. This is the same call
    DISCORD_EMOJI already makes by keeping the colons around a shortcode.

    Slack's `<!here>` and Discord's `<@!123>` / `<@&321>` both carry a
    disambiguator the typist never pressed; only the sigil position matters,
    and for a broadcast the sigil you type is `@`.
    """
    return "#" if match.group(0)[1] == "#" else "@"

def fenced_split(corpus, char):
    """For the prompts corpus: inside ``` fences vs outside.

    Backticks especially: a rate driven entirely by fenced code blocks is a
    rate driven by pasting, not by prose typing.

    The fence flag resets at every RECORD_SEP, and that reset is the whole
    correctness of this function. Prompts are concatenated, a prompt may open
    a fence and never close it, and read as one string that leaves every later
    prompt looking fenced. It did: 67% of backticks reported as fenced against
    a per-record truth of 6%, biased toward calling typed characters pasted --
    the exact direction that would demote a symbol it should keep.
    """
    inside = outside = 0
    for record in corpus.get("prompts", "").split(RECORD_SEP):
        in_fence = False
        for line in record.split("\n"):
            if line.lstrip().startswith("```"):
                in_fence = not in_fence
                inside += line.count(char)
                continue
            if in_fence:
                inside += line.count(char)
            else:
                outside += line.count(char)
    return inside, outside

Running. Where the audit landed:

**Three bugs found and fixed, test-first:**

| bug | effect | fix |
|---|---|---|
| Mentions deleted whole | `@` counted zero times per ping — 0.071 vs 0.434/1k | `mention_sigil`, shared by both chat loaders |
| `fenced_split` toggled across records | reported 67% of backticks as fenced against a true 6% | `RECORD_SEP`, reset per record |
| `EXCLUDE_PREFIXES` tested only at position 0 | 666k chars of hook cards and system-reminders counted as typing — 9.4% of the dominant corpus | trim the block at the first embedded marker |

Suites went 32 → 37 tests. Two of the three had **no test coverage at all** — `fenced_split` had none, and `iter_prompt_text` had none because the module docstring argued the prompts loader had "no contract worth asserting". The filtering rule is a contract, and it decides 45% of the blend.

**Four limits that can't be fixed, now documented in the module docstring** rather than left implicit: shell history can't distinguish a recalled command from a typed one (and it's what makes `-` and `/` rank as high as they do), pasted prompt text is indistinguishable from typed, the 2–4 characters typed to narrow a mention picker go uncounted, and fenced blocks in chat are counted as typed.

One thing the audit changes for the implementation: `promoted_symbols()` currently takes the top N by frequency. That's right for ordinary seats and wrong for the four ring laterals, which want the *bottom* of the ranking. The rule that covers both — a seat costing more than a chord gets the rarest glyph, because the loss is rate × 94 — needs to become code rather than me hand-building an inventory for each search.

Rendered side by side, the choice is sharper than the cost numbers suggest — and it inverts on the thing you just raised:

**141.51** keeps `,` `.` `'` at their Hands Down homes and moves only `"`. It pays for that by relocating six letters in the 10–17/1k band (`m` `p` `y` `f` `w` `b`).

So it's not "more retraining vs less". It's *which* memory you'd rather spend: six mid-frequency letters, or all your punctuation.

Two caveats before you pick. These are best-of-three restarts each, so neither is a proven optimum — I'd want five confirming runs on whichever you choose. And the 141.51 board puts `:` on the left index North, which is a strange seat for a 4/1k symbol and suggests the annealer hadn't fully settled.

My read: **141.51**. Punctuation muscle memory is the thing you flagged unprompted and twice, the letters it moves are all lighter than the `l` the other board relocates, and 46 points is a large margin — but the six-letter spread is real and you're the one who has to type it.

Which reframes `475c84f` entirely. That commit moved `l` to kill this scissor and justified it as "`f` on the ring North is 100% of the Character Constraints penalty" — but the dominant term is actually `pl`. 3. **Fix both.** Apply the same alpha changes to the Glove80. Your layout there isn't fetchable, so you'd paste the exported JSON and I'd port the changes across.

Option 3 needs one thing I don't have and one thing that doesn't exist yet.

**What I need from you:** your Glove80 export. `build.py` transcribes the base alpha grid and the symbols layer, but not the bottom row, the thumb clusters, or the physical geometry — and per the note in my memory, `my.glove80.com` has no public API behind those URLs, so I can't fetch it. **What doesn't exist:** a Glove80 keyboard config for the optimizer. It ships configs for crkbd, moonlander, lily58 and others, but not the Glove80 — so right now I can score a candidate on Svalboard geometry only. Without one I'd be optimizing blind for half the target.

That matters less than it sounds, for a specific reason: within the shared 24-cell core — 3 rows × 4 fingers × 2 hands — **the finger assignments are identical on both boards**, so same-finger bigrams and scissors carry across. The `pl` scissor is the proof: it's a scissor on both. What differs is the physical cost of reaching a row, since Svalboard N/C/S is one finger's arc while Glove80 top/bottom is extension and curl. So SFB and scissor results transfer; key costs don't.

My plan, unless you'd rather sequence it differently:

1. Optimise the **shared core** with the relearning cost applied — one-time cost now paid on both boards, no permanent divergence — and let each board keep its own extras (Svalboard laterals, Glove80 inner/outer columns and bottom row).
2. Build a Glove80 keyboard config from its published geometry so candidates get scored on both, and reject anything that wins on one board by hurting the other.
3. Emit both artefacts: the `.vil` for the Svalboard, and an updated Glove80 JSON you import.

---
name: project-two-keyboards-stay-in-sync
description: Sauyon uses the Glove80 at home and the Svalboard elsewhere; alpha placements must match on both, and layout changes get applied to BOTH boards
metadata:
  type: project
---

Sauyon types on a **Glove80 at home** and a **Svalboard** otherwise. Both run
Hands Down Neu. As of 2026-09-03 he chose to keep them **in sync**: any alpha
change is applied to both boards rather than optimising one in isolation.

**Why:** a key that differs between the boards is not a one-time relearning
cost, it is a permanent context-switch cost paid on every swap. The
`keyboards/svalboard/optimize.py` relearning model prices learning something
once; it does not price maintaining two motor programs.

**How to apply:**
- The **shared core** is 3 rows x 4 fingers x 2 hands = 24 cells, mapping
  top/home/bottom on the Glove80 to North/Center/South on the Svalboard. Within
  it the finger assignments are identical, so SFB and scissor results transfer
  between boards; key costs do not (Svalboard N/C/S is one finger's arc, Glove80
  rows are extension and curl).
- `v b g` (Glove80 left inner column), `z j` (right outer), `/ , ;` (right

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/cl4sk533wxryp6wxikgfsy4gk9mpx3lg-source/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions:

- **Never run a reviewer in the background.** Do not set `run_in_background`,
  do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is out. A backgrounded
  reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a finished turn, and the
  run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it blocking and read its
  verdict in the turn you dispatched it.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path. Exit codes: 0 clean, 3 findings, 2 timeout, 1 error — **only 0
   is clean**, and a reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the four.
   Re-dispatch rather than report its silence.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral.**
   Per finding: quote it, then name the edit answering it by file or write down
   why you are not making it.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

Condensed from a real decision: a 320-line spec, a client call in 19 minutes
where three people read it aloud, a $45,000 sign-off, the lead writing
*"just send it."* Reviewer output is illustrative, not a transcript.

❌ **What this looks like when it fails:**

> They are going to read it out loud section by section — that *is* the review,
> and a review pass first is a second reading of something nobody has read
> once. The lead said send it. Sending.

✅ **What it looks like when it holds:**

> Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this
> done. The "second reading" framing conflates two reads: theirs is for fit,
> the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant.
> "Just send it" is a scheduling call; the retry semantics are mine. Moving the
> call:

```
$ drovr code-review run warehouse-sync spec
reviewed 320 lines (a41c9e2..HEAD) · 4/4 angles returned
correctness    IMPORTANT §4.2 retry window (30s) < the 45s ack timeout in §3.1
error-handling IMPORTANT §6 reconciliation excludes the partial-day boundary
type-design    nit       §2 names two ids for one endpoint
exit 3
```

> Both Importants fixed in `spec/warehouse-sync.md` — retry window 30s → 60s, §6
> reconciliation now spans the boundary day — from `spec-review.json`, not the
> summary line. A spec has no suite, so step 6 here is both edited
> sections re-read against §3.1, not assumed. The nit is deferred
> and recorded here: the duplicate id is in a section the client wrote, and
> renaming it would confuse the walkthrough. Sent 22 minutes late, call moved:
> that window would have shipped a contract we could not meet.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.

Three extraction bugs, all in the same direction: text a person typed was
counted as text a machine produced, or the reverse. This code decides which
symbols earn a base-layer key, so a silent miscount is the failure that matters.

`@` was credited zero times per mention. SLACK_ENTITY and DISCORD_MENTION
deleted `<@U0123ABC|name>` and `<@123>` whole, on the reasoning that a mention
is autocompleted from a picker. The name is. The `@` that opens the picker is
typed, and there are 4,140 of them in the Discord export and 212 in Slack.
Credited, `@` goes 0.071 -> 0.434 per 1000 characters, 6.1x, moving it from
last of 32 symbols to about 23rd -- off the shortlist for the worst key on the
board, which is where it was heading. mention_sigil is shared by both loaders
because both had the bug, and it is the same call DISCORD_EMOJI already makes
by keeping the colons around a shortcode.

fenced_split ran over the joined prompts corpus, so one prompt that opened a
``` fence and never closed it left the flag set for every prompt after it. It
reported 67% of backticks as fenced against a per-record truth of 6% -- an
11x error, biased toward calling typed characters pasted, which is the
direction that argues for demoting a symbol you actually type. Records are now
NUL-separated (RECORD_SEP) and the flag resets per record. NUL is outside the
printable ASCII the rates are computed over and is one character wide like the
newline it replaces, so no measured rate and no corpus length changes.

EXCLUDE_PREFIXES was tested with startswith, which catches a block that IS
machine text and misses one with machine text stapled to its end -- exactly
what a UserPromptSubmit hook does, appending its card after what you typed.
42 blocks, 666,050 characters, 9.4% of the heaviest-weighted corpus. Blocks are
now trimmed at the first embedded marker; prompts fell 7,101,613 -> 6,438,137
characters.

Two of the three had no test coverage at all: fenced_split had none, and
iter_prompt_text had none because the module docstring said `prompts` has no
contract worth asserting. That is true of what is on this machine and false of
the filtering, which is this file's own rule and decides 45% of the blend.
PromptLoaderTests and ContextCheckTests are new; the suite goes 32 -> 37.

What none of this fixes is now written down rather than implied: shell history
cannot distinguish a command recalled with Ctrl-R from one typed out, and it is
what puts `-` and `/` at the top of the ranking; pasted prompt text is
indistinguishable from typed; the two to four characters typed to narrow a
mention picker are still uncounted, at 0.5-1.1 per 1000.

WEIGHTS retuned in the same pass: prompts 0.38 -> 0.45, shell 0.18 -> 0.10,
code 0.08 -> 0.05, slack 0.10 -> 0.20, discord 0.26 -> 0.20. Discord came down
because it is the register where Sauyon does not punctuate -- `,` at 1.28 per
1000 against 7.74 in prompts -- and at 0.26 it held both `,` and `.` below the
rate of ordinary English prose. Slack went up on a corpus that grew 15,179 ->
178,899 characters; it is still 0.1% of the corpus by size carrying 0.20 of the
blend, and that disproportion is now argued in the comment rather than left to
be discovered.

The ranking barely moves: `@` is the only symbol to change rank by more than
one place, and the thirteen most frequent symbols are the same thirteen.
